text.en: In 1911 the sociologist Howard Odum printed songs he had heard in Mississippi and Georgia. Of one, about Joe Turner, he wrote: "Each line is sung three times to make a stanza."
text.es: En 1911, el sociólogo Howard Odum publicó canciones que había oído en Misisipi y Georgia. De una, sobre Joe Turner, escribió: "Cada verso se canta tres veces para formar una estrofa."

source.en: Odum, Journal of American Folk-Lore 24 (1911), p. 351, Internet Archive
source.es: Odum, Journal of American Folk-Lore 24 (1911), p. 351, Internet Archive

text.en: Blind Willie Johnson's 1927 recording of Dark Was the Night, Cold Was the Ground has no words, only hums and moans over his slide guitar. In 1977 NASA put it on the Voyager Golden Record.

text.en: W. C. Handy found the folk habit of singing one line three times too monotonous. So in St. Louis Blues he made a statement, repeated it, then used the last line to tell "why the statement was made."
text.es: A W. C. Handy le parecía demasiado monótona la costumbre popular de cantar un verso tres veces. Así que en St. Louis Blues hizo una afirmación, la repitió y usó el último verso para contar "por qué se había hecho la afirmación".

source.en: Handy, Father of the Blues (New York: Macmillan, 1941), pp. 142-143, Internet Archive
source.es: Handy, Father of the Blues (New York: Macmillan, 1941), pp. 142-143, Internet Archive

text.en: In 1903 an archaeologist who had dug a mound in Coahoma County, Mississippi, wrote that his crew often sang a refrain's final home note a little sharp: "So frequent was this that it seemed intentional or unavoidable, not merely a mistake in pitch."
text.es: En 1903, un arqueólogo que había excavado un túmulo en el condado de Coahoma (Misisipi) escribió que su cuadrilla solía cantar la nota base final de un estribillo un poco por encima: "Era tan frecuente que parecía intencionado o inevitable, no un simple error de afinación."

source.en: Peabody, Journal of American Folk-Lore 16 (1903), p. 151, Internet Archive
source.es: Peabody, Journal of American Folk-Lore 16 (1903), p. 151, Internet Archive

text.en: Muscle Shoals Blues, printed in 1921, begs "go with me to Muscle Shoals". That year Henry Ford offered to lease the unfinished dam and plants there, setting off a short-lived land boom.
text.es: Muscle Shoals Blues, publicado en 1921, suplica "go with me to Muscle Shoals". Ese año, Henry Ford se ofreció a arrendar la presa sin terminar y las fábricas de la zona, y desató una fiebre por los terrenos que duró poco.

source.en: Encyclopedia of Alabama, "Muscle Shoals"; The Henry Ford museum; Mississippi State University Libraries

text.en: In the folk blues, W. C. Handy wrote, the singer filled occasional gaps with words like "Oh, baby". In St. Louis Blues he filled those gaps in the piano and orchestra parts instead. Such a fill is called a break.
text.es: En el blues tradicional, escribió W. C. Handy, el cantante rellenaba algún hueco con palabras como "Oh, baby". En St. Louis Blues, él rellenó esos huecos con el piano y la orquesta. A ese relleno se le llama break.

source.en: Handy, Father of the Blues (New York: Macmillan, 1941), pp. 120-121, Internet Archive
source.es: Handy, Father of the Blues (New York: Macmillan, 1941), pp. 120-121, Internet Archive

text.en: Waiting for a late train at Tutwiler, Mississippi, W. C. Handy woke to a guitarist pressing a knife on his strings as he played. Handy called the effect unforgettable.
text.es: Mientras esperaba un tren con retraso en Tutwiler (Misisipi), W. C. Handy se despertó al oír a un guitarrista que tocaba apoyando un cuchillo en las cuerdas. Handy dijo que aquel efecto era inolvidable.

text.en: The Fives, by George W. Thomas and his brother Hersal, was inspired by railroad travel. George said he based its piano left hand on the rhythm of the trains.

text.en: Waking up this morning was sung about long before blues records. A camp workers' song Howard Odum printed in 1911 sings three times of waking up this morning and not being able to keep from crying, then answers it.

text.en: Hersal Thomas, who wrote The Fives with his much older brother George, was a piano prodigy whose playing of it inspired Chicago pianists such as Albert Ammons and Meade Lux Lewis. He died suddenly in Detroit in 1926, still in his teens.

text.en: In Coahoma County, Mississippi, in 1901 and 1902, an archaeologist heard his crew make up lines on the spot about whatever was going on. One Saturday half-holiday, a sing-song came out of the trench: Mighty long half day, Captain.
text.es: En el condado de Coahoma (Misisipi), en 1901 y 1902, un arqueólogo oyó a su cuadrilla inventar versos sobre la marcha acerca de lo que estuviera pasando. Un sábado en que solo se trabajaba media jornada, salió de la zanja una cantinela: "Mighty long half day, Captain".

source.en: Peabody, Journal of American Folk-Lore 16 (1903), pp. 149-150, Internet Archive
